3. **InkDiT: An Efficient Conditional Latent Diffusion for Handwritten Text-Line Generation**

Building on top of InkVAE, we further design InkDiT, a **novel latent-space diffusion Transformer** that generates high-quality stylized handwritten text lines conditioned on both textual content and writing style. InkDiT incorporates a **lightweight content encoder** that adaptively projects the input text sequence into the latent feature space, ensuring that long text lines are modeled efficiently. The **style conditions are extracted directly from the pretrained InkVAE encoder**, eliminating the need for an additional standalone style encoder and enabling efficient conditional diffusion modeling within a unified latent representation space.

Our ablation studies demonstrate that the lightweight content encoder substantially improves content accuracy in the generated text while introducing minimal computational overhead. As shown in the table below, although this module incurs a slight reduction in generation speed (from 71.94 char/s to 58.47 char/s), it leads to a significant gain in both content accuracy and style consistency: **the average content accuracy increases from 81\% to 94\% (+13\%), and the style score improves from 65.49 to 77.38.**

- *W2: Can DiffInk Support More Complex Forms of Style Conditioning?*

DiffInk uses a continuous handwritten segment as the style reference to produce a text line with consistent stylistic characteristics, following prior text-line generation approaches [1][2]. However, **DiffInk can support more complex forms of style input**, we conducted an exploration at the feature level. Specifically, we encode reference trajectories from two different writers using the VAE to obtain two latent style representations. These representations are then combined through weighted averaging to form a new mixed-style features, which is used as the contextual condition for generating the subsequent text line. The results are included in Figure 11 on page 19 of the appendix in the revised PDF, demonstrate that DiffInk can successfully support style mixing and generate stylistic variations beyond the original training distribution.


---

- *W3&Q3 — Image-based text conditioning*

Thank you for raising this valuable point. Using image-based encodings to provide structural information for characters has indeed been well explored in character stylization research. However, extending this idea to long and complex text-line generation remains largely underexplored. The main challenge lies in the fact that text lines involve not only character-level structural cues but also positional and size variations—information that is difficult to obtain from existing character templates.

To investigate the feasibility of image-based text conditioning for OOV scenarios in long text lines, we conducted a preliminary exploration. We first prepared a glyph library (Heiti.ttf), covering more than 10k Chinese and English characters, and rendered each required character as an image. We then evaluated two ways of extracting content features from these images:

**1) Full-line template encoding:** Render the entire text line as a single template image and extract its representation using an image encoder. **2) Per-character encoding with spatial concatenation:**  Render each character individually, encode each using an image encoder, concatenate the features in character order along the spatial dimension, and then apply positional encoding to form a text-line representation. All character images were rendered at 128×128 resolution, and the encoder used was a ResNet-18. We retrained DiffInk under both image-based conditioning schemes and evaluated performance accordingly.

### Quantitative results under different textual conditioning strategies

| Single Image + ResNet-18     | 86.79     | 86.92     | 65.81       | 1.231     | 50.10             |
| **Embedding + ConvNeXt-V2 (Ours)**      | **94.38**     | **94.58**     | **77.38**       | **1.049**     | **58.47**             |

From the quantitative results, both image-based approaches underperform the embedding-based method, particularly the full-line template encoding, which increases computational cost while yielding lower accuracy. Although image-based text conditioning is generally more flexible in handling diverse text inputs, **it is also sensitive to template font selection, encoder design, and the way text conditions are aligned with the latent diffusion process**, requiring careful engineering to be effective in text-line generation.

DiffInk directly incorporates textual embeddings into the VAE latent space as conditioning signals. **This approach has been shown to be more effective than designing separate conditional control modules**, as demonstrated in recent studies [3][4]. **It enables content semantics and structural features to be jointly modeled within a unified representation space.** Designing a more general text-conditioning mechanism (e.g., image-based inputs or universal text-encoder inputs) will be an important direction for our future work.

We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments and the valuable feedback. - *W1: Regarding the concern that the overall framework appears to be a combination of existing techniques.*

**Use of latent diffusion models.**

DiffInk differs substantially from [1] in **both modeling paradigm and technical implementation.** In [1], content and layout are decoupled, and two U-Net–based diffusion models are trained in separate stages: (1) one model predicts the character-level bounding boxes along a text line, and (2) another model stylizes the text-line template using the predicted character bounding boxes. The key point is that, the method in [1] employs **two separate latent diffusion models to guide content and style generation independently**, making the overall pipeline relatively complex and difficult to follow.

In contrast, we proposes a novel modeling paradigm: an **end-to-end handwritten text-line generator that models both content and style jointly within a unified latent diffusion Transformer.** The design is conceptually simple, easy to understand and reproduce, and demonstrates strong empirical performance. Beyond directly applying latent diffusion, we introduce InkVAE—featuring glyph-aware and style-aware regularization—to address the core challenges of content accuracy and style consistency in long-sequence handwriting generation. Extensive ablations verify the effectiveness of this design.

We would like to clarify that the publication date of this paper[1] is very close to ICLR’s submission deadline, so it was not possible for DiffInk to adopt its technical designs. In addition, the two methods differ significantly in both motivation and implementation details.

**Similarity in text encoding strategies.**

Using embedding-based textual representations to guide handwriting generation has been widely validated as an effective strategy in prior work [3][4][5]. DiffInk also adopts an embedding-based representation for textual content; however, its application scenario and underlying design philosophy differ substantially from those of method [2] referenced by the reviewer. 

Although both methods represent textual content using embeddings, their alignment designs and objectives are fundamentally different. We think that, in our scenario, the proposed approach is more flexible, and the ablation studies further demonstrate its effectiveness.
In [2], the embedding of each character is repeated multiple times to align its temporal dimension with the style-related tokens. In [2], the embeddings of characters are **simply repeated to align with the style features, and a feature fusion mechanism** is then applied to generate the corresponding handwritten results. In our framework, we instead pad the character embedding sequence **to a unified dimensionality and employ a lightweight content encoder** based on ConvNeXtV2 to provide content feature conditions for the diffusion model, guiding it to generate the corresponding results. 

**Summary.**

Overall, DiffInk introduces the first end-to-end framework for handwritten text-line generation built upon a general latent diffusion model. The design is novel, coherent, and well motivated, providing a general framework that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the highly challenging task of complex Chinese handwriting synthesis.We believe that DiffInk makes meaningful advances in both modeling paradigm and key technical components.

- *Q3: Regarding the Potential Effects of Synthetic Data*

We analyze the necessity and rationale of incorporating synthetic data in our work, as well as its impact on the overall model performance.

---

**1. Synthetic Data as an Effective and Common Strategy for Data Augmentation**

Due to the limitations of real-world handwriting data in terms of both scale and diversity, many OCR-related generation and recognition methods leverage synthetic data for augmentation. Synthetic data often provide a more balanced character distribution and richer stylistic variability, effectively compensating for the deficiencies of real datasets. Among existing approaches, some methods [1,2] train directly on large-scale synthetic datasets and achieve state-of-the-art performance when evaluated on real handwriting. In addition, a more common practice adopted in prior work [3,4] is to construct hybrid training sets that combine real and synthetic data, thereby improving model performance and robustness in real-world inference scenarios. Following this paradigm, our DiffInk model is also trained using a mixture of real and synthetic data and is ultimately evaluated on real handwriting.

---

**2. Analyzing the Impact of Synthetic Data on Model Performance**

By analyzing the real handwritten text-line dataset, we observe a pronounced long-tail distribution across character categories: each writer exhibits substantial variation in character usage and writing frequency. As a result, common characters appear frequently, whereas rare or less commonly used characters occur only a few times. Such a long-tail distribution leads to insufficient learning of content representations for low-frequency characters, ultimately degrading the model’s generation capability.

To mitigate this issue, following prior work [3,4,5], we incorporate synthetic data to compensate for the imbalance in character frequency. Specifically, we construct a mixed training set that combines both real and synthetic text lines. We train the model under different data settings and evaluate all variants on the same real-world test set. As shown in the table, the model trained solely on real data achieves only moderate performance (average content accuracy of 81\% and style score of 68.95). In contrast, **augmenting the training set with synthetic data substantially improves performance: content accuracy increases to 94\% (+13\%), and the style score increases to 77.38 (+8.43).** These results indicate that synthetic data effectively alleviates the character long-tail issue, enabling the model to better learn character-level representations. Moreover, exposure to more diverse character combinations enhances the model’s robustness in style modeling.

**3. Fine-tuning the DiffInk (Ours) on real data**

We also understand the reviewer’s concern regarding the potential negative impact of synthetic data on temporal continuity modeling. **To address this issue, we designed a simple yet effective mitigation strategy.** During training, we continue to use a mixture of real and synthetic data, ensuring that characters in the long-tail distribution are sufficiently learned. **After the model converges, we perform a brief fine-tuning stage using only real data (about 1,000 steps)**, allowing the model to quickly adapt to the real-data distribution.

We then evaluate the fine-tuned model on the real test set. As shown in the table, **the style score further increases from 77.38 to 78.11 (+0.73)**, indicating that **the potential adverse effects introduced by synthetic data can be effectively mitigated through lightweight fine-tuning on real handwriting.** This strategy is also consistent with prior studies[4], which similarly adopt real-data fine-tuning to mitigate the domain gap between synthetic and real samples.

---

In summary, the use of **synthetic data is necessary** because it substantially **alleviates the long-tail sparsity inherent in real handwriting datasets.**
Although synthetic samples inevitably differ from real data in distribution, their use introduces only **limited adverse effects** when combined with real data during training. 1. **Incremental Nature of the Core Technical Contribution**  
   While the empirical results are robust, the core technical innovation can be characterized more as a skillful integration and refinement of existing components (VAE, DiT) rather than a groundbreaking algorithmic advancement.

   The reliance on a data augmentation strategy that stitches isolated characters into text lines presents a significant methodological limitation. This approach inherently fails to capture the cursive connections and natural co-articulation found in real handwritten text, which likely imposes a ceiling on the model’s ability to generate fully authentic, fluid text lines and raises questions about the underlying sources of its performance gains.
